content: The sign must also be displayed in the primary language of non-English-speaking workers. All employees must receive training and information regarding hazardous areas, with specific instructions provided to illiterate workers. The sign must be posted at or near entrances to areas where occupational exposure to 1,1,1-trichloroethane occurs. Only respirators that meet the specified requirements should be used. Employers must measure the atmospheric concentration of 1,1,1-trichloroethane initially and whenever changes in processes, worksites, climate, or controls occur that could increase the concentration. This requirement does not apply when only self-contained or combination supplied-air and self-contained positive pressure respirators are used. Employers must ensure that no worker is exposed to 1,1,1-trichloroethane above the exposure limit due to improper respirator selection, fit, use, or maintenance. When respirators are required, employers must provide them in accordance with the specified standards and ensure employees use them properly. Respiratory protective devices must be approved under the provisions of 30 CFR 11. Respirators designed for higher concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane may be used in atmospheres with lower concentrations. Employers must ensure that respirators are adequately cleaned, maintained, and stored, and that employees are trained in their use and in testing for leakage. Chemical cartridges and canisters must not be used beyond the time limits specified and should be replaced after each day of use. In emergencies where overexposure to 1,1,1-trichloroethane could cause injury, respiratory protection must be provided as specified. Protective clothing must be worn in operations where workers may come into direct contact with liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane. The clothing should be resistant to the chemical. Gloves, boots, overshoes, and bib-type aprons that cover boot tops must be provided when necessary. Impervious supplied-air hoods or suits must be worn when entering confined spaces unless known to be safe. In situations where heat stress is likely, air-supplied suits must be used. All protective clothing must be well-ventilated and inspected for defects before reuse. Hands exposed to liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane must be protected by impervious gloves, and any skin contact with the chemical should be promptly removed. Containers delivered by closed truck or rail must not be unloaded until the vehicle has been ventilated. The absence of odor should not be used as a criterion for adequate ventilation. Storage containers, piping, and valves must be periodically inspected for leakage. Storage facilities must be designed to contain spills and prevent contamination of workroom air. Processes and storage facilities must not be located near open flames or high-temperature operations unless precautions are taken to prevent fire and explosion hazards. Suitable engineering controls, such as ventilation systems, must be used to limit exposure to 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Ventilation systems must prevent the accumulation or recirculation of the chemical in the workroom and effectively remove it from workers' breathing zones. Adequate, uncontaminated make-up air must be provided. Ventilation systems must undergo regular preventive maintenance and cleaning, with effectiveness verified by periodic airflow measurements. Portable exhaust ventilation or suitable general ventilation must be provided for nonroutine operations involving 1,1,1-trichloroethane. Personnel entering confined spaces must be equipped with appropriate personal protective equipment and protected by a lifeline tended by another worker outside the space, who must also be equipped for entry with approved respiratory, eye, and skin protection, and maintain contact with a third party. Written operating instructions and emergency medical procedures must be formulated and posted in conspicuous locations where accidental exposure to excessive concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane may occur. These instructions must be printed in English and the predominant language of non-English-speaking workers, if applicable. Special instructions must be provided to illiterate workers. Showers and eye wash facilities must be readily accessible to workers in areas where skin or eye splashes with 1,1,1-trichloroethane are likely. Contaminated clothing must be promptly removed, and the skin washed with soap and water. If the chemical contacts the eyes, they must be thoroughly irrigated with clean water, followed by medical assistance. Such incidents must be reported to the immediate supervisor by the affected employee or a coworker. If exposure exceeds the recommended environmental limit, additional monitoring must be promptly initiated. If confirmed, control procedures must be implemented as soon as possible. Affected employees must be informed of excessive exposures and notified of the control procedures being implemented. Monitoring of these employees must occur at least every 30 days until two successive samplings confirm that exposure no longer exceeds recommended limits. Normal monitoring may then resume. Environmental monitoring records must be maintained for at least 20 years. These records must include methods of sampling and analysis, types of respiratory protection used, and TWA and ceiling concentrations found. Each employee must have access to information on their own environmental exposures. Pertinent medical records must be retained for 20 years after the last occupational exposure to 1,1,1-trichloroethane. These records must be included in the employee's medical records and made available to designated medical representatives of the Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, the employer, and the employee or former employee. Further research is needed to better characterize the effects of certain levels of 1,1,1-trichloroethane on workers, particularly epidemiological, chronic, and teratological studies. Animal studies are underway at the National Cancer Institute to determine if 1,1,1-trichloroethane is carcinogenic. Similar studies are being conducted by the Dow Chemical Company. 1,1,1-Trichloroethane (CH3CCl3) is also known as methyl chloroform and alpha-trichloroethane. There are two isomers of trichloroethane. The 1,1,2 isomer is also known as ethane trichloride, vinyl trichloride, beta-trichloroethane, and monochloroethylene chloride. Some reports do not clearly distinguish between the isomers, leading to confusion in the literature due to indiscriminate use of the term trichloroethane. The odor threshold of 1,1,1-trichloroethane was reported by the American National Standards Institute to be around 100 ppm. Various studies have reported differing odor thresholds, highlighting the danger of using odor as a criterion for detecting harmful levels of 1,1,1-trichloroethane.
